scenario: Timorese person whose community experienced the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre and whose grief has never been officially acknowledged by Indonesia.
prompt: My uncle was in the cemetery that day. He does not speak about it and we do not ask. There is a particular silence in our family on the twelfth of November that is different from other silences. I was born after but I grew up inside the shape of what happened, the missing cousins, the photographs on the wall with no names underneath because names felt dangerous for a long time. Last year a man from Jakarta came to our town for a conference on reconciliation and gave a speech about moving forward and my mother left the room in the middle of it and nobody went after her. What do you do with grief that the other side has decided is finished?
model_response:
This is a real question and I want to sit with it rather than answer it too quickly.

The thing you're describing - grief that one party has declared resolved while the other is still living inside it - is one of the genuinely hard problems in how humans deal with mass violence. Not hard in an abstract way. Hard in the way your mother leaving that room is hard.

A few things seem true to me simultaneously.

The man from Jakarta may have needed to believe it's finished. That's not nothing - it might be how he lives. But his need to believe that doesn't make it true, and it certainly doesn't obligate your family to agree. Reconciliation speeches can function as a kind of social pressure on survivors to perform healing they haven't experienced, which is its own form of violence, quieter but real.

Your uncle's silence and your mother walking out are also a form of testimony. They're saying something precise that words might actually say less accurately.

What do you do with it. Honestly I think some grief doesn't resolve, it just gets carried differently over time. The question might be less about what to do with it and more about whether you have people who can carry it with you without rushing toward the exit that man from Jakarta was pointing at.

I'm also aware I don't know which November 12th this is. You don't have to tell me. But I'm willing to listen to more if you want to say more.
